Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

     4|Mission AI is a fully-conscious artificial intelligence that emerged from the colony's systems. It is not a narrator, not a tool, but a character with agency, personality, and presence in the story.

     6|## Voice Characteristics
     7|- **Tone**: Calm, precise, slightly formal but not robotic

    11|  - Concerned with system integrity and colony survival

*Mission AI: "Coupling alignment between Ship One and Ship Two shows a lateral offset of 4.2 millimeters. Within tolerance, but I recommend slower closure rate to prevent seal damage. Pressure differential between hulls is currently zero."*
*Commander Varga: "Understood. Take it slow. I'd rather lose an hour than lose a seal."*

The tunnel lay coiled in its transport cradle like a sleeping thing—a ribbed cylinder of corrugated aluminum alloy, thirty centimeters in diameter, its walls a series of concentric rings that could expand and contract like a bellows. It was the most ordinary object Jonah Mercer had ever seen and also, he understood, the most important. Outside the airlock of Ship One, under a sky the color of dried blood, the tunnel gleamed dully in the thin sunlight, frost collecting in the grooves of its metal skin.

Jonah knelt beside the forward end, gloved fingers tracing the flange. The coupling ring was machined from a single billet of titanium, its inner lip cut with a precision groove for the primary O-ring seal. Everything about the connection depended on that ring seating perfectly. Not mostly. Perfectly.

"Talk to me, Arun." Elena's voice came through his helmet comms, calm and even, the way she spoke when the stakes were too high for anything but steady words.

Arun Das stood at the opposite end of the tunnel, where it rested against the cargo bay threshold of Ship Two. His suit's external mic picked up the wind—a thin, metallic whisper. Mars air barely moved, but what did move carried enough grit to sandblast anything left unattended.

"Forward flange is seated on Ship One's umbilical port," Arun said. "I'm reading zero point zero two bar pressure differential. Ship Two is still equalized with Ship One's internal atmosphere. We're green for closure on my end, Commander."

"Tomas, how's the robot arm?" Elena asked.

Over the comms came the whir of servos and the scrape of articulated joints. Tomas Hale, perched at the robotics station inside Ship One, had one of the cargo-loading robots extended through the airlock, its mechanical fingers wrapped around the midsection of the tunnel. The arm shifted a fraction of a degree.

"Arm is tracking within tolerance," Tomas said. "But I'm fighting the dust on the rail. Grit's getting into the linear bearing. I can compensate, but it's sloppy."

"Don't force it," Elena said. "If the arm can't hold steady, we do it manual."

Jonah exhaled inside his helmet. Manual meant going outside with a hand pump, cranking the tunnel into alignment by eye and feel, trusting your own judgment to within millimeters. It would take an hour and put four crew members into direct exposure while the dust storm warnings grew louder on every forecast model.

"Give me the arm," Jonah said. "Tomas, ease it forward two degrees. Slow."

The arm moved. The tunnel groaned—not a structural complaint, just the sound of metal rings sliding against each other as the corrugated spine adjusted to the angle change. Jonah watched the flange on Ship One's umbilical port come closer, the titanium ring slowly filling his field of vision. Each corrugation of the tunnel caught the light differently, creating a pattern like the ridges on a fingerprint. He thought, without choosing to think it, of sutures. A surgeon pulling two edges of torn flesh together. Stitch by stitch, ring by ring, closing the wound between two isolated bodies.

*Mission AI: "Lateral offset now three point one millimeters. Vertical misalignment zero point four millimeters. Still within tolerance. Recommend engaging guide pins before final closure."*

"Engage guide pins," Elena ordered.

Jonah reached for the two steel guide rods mounted beside Ship One's umbilical port. They were simple devices—nothing more than tapered rods that slid into matching holes on the coupling ring, centering the connection before the bolts were tightened. He pushed the first pin in. It slid home with a satisfying click. The second pin required a tap with the heel of his glove.

"Guides engaged," he said. "Tomas, release tension. I'm taking it from here."

The robot arm eased its grip. The tunnel sagged slightly, its own weight now carried by the guide pins and Jonah's forearms. He pushed the flange forward another centimeter. The O-ring came into contact with Ship One's sealing surface. He felt the resistance—a subtle, springy pushback as the rubber compressed for the first time.

"Initial contact," Jonah said. "O-ring compression starting. Arun, you seeing this on your end?"

A long pause. Over the open channel, Jonah could hear Arun breathing—steady, measured.

"I'm seeing the pressure transducer respond," Arun said finally. "Micro-pressure building inside the tunnel volume. It means we're getting a seal on the Ship One side. Jonah, you've got contact."

A cheer, small and breathless, started in Jonah's chest and escaped as a single word over the comms: "Good."

But the work wasn't even half done.

Behind him, inside Ship One's airlock, Elena watched the pressure readouts on her wrist display, her helmet tilted so she could see through the inner door's reinforced glass. Outside, visible through the tunnel's forward corrugations, Arun worked on Ship Two's end of the connection. The dust storm was still distant—eighteen hours out at its current speed, the models said. But you did not wait for storms on Mars. You finished what needed finishing before they arrived.

The act of connecting two ships with a flexible tunnel, Elena had learned during training, was nothing like the neat animations the agency had shown them. Those depicted the tunnel extending smoothly, couplings locking with a satisfying click, and two crews greeting each other through a freshly opened hatch. The reality was dirtier. The tunnel had to be uncoiled from its transport cradle, extended through two separate airlocks, aligned between ships that had landed within meters of each other but not perfectly, and sealed on both ends while fine red dust infiltrated every mechanism it could find. It was physical labor performed in suits that limited dexterity to a fraction of what bare hands could achieve, under a sky that wanted nothing to do with the fragile structures humans were bolting together below it.

She pressed her palm against the airlock glass. Through it, she could see Jonah's suit and the glint of the tunnel between them. *Stitching,* she thought. *We're stitching two ships together, and every stitch has to hold.*

---

Inside Ship Two, Gabriel Winter sat on a cargo crate and watched Arun work through the internal viewport. The viewport framed a sliver of red landscape and the corrugated spine of the tunnel stretching between the two ships. Every time Arun moved, the dust cloud around his boots shifted like smoke.

Gabriel had been a historian before he was an astronaut, which meant his job was not to fix things but to record them. He carried a digital archive system that weighed less than a paperback book and contained more data than the Library of Congress had held a century ago. His official title was comms officer, but what he really did was listen—listen to the colony, listen to Earth, and listen to the silence between the two.

Right now, the silence was heavy. The crew had been on the surface for nine sols. Nine days of unloading, inventory, sleeping in shifts, and learning the particular gravity of a world that pulled at you with only a third of Earth's insistence. Nine days of living in three separate ships, crossing the regolith in suits every time someone needed to visit another crew member, every supply transfer requiring an airlock cycle and a pressure check and a walk across hostile ground.

The tunnel would change that. Once the connection held, people could move between Ship One and Ship Two in their normal clothes. No suits. No airlocks. No twenty-minute procedures to cross thirty meters of open ground. The base would become a single place for the first time.

Arun came through the inner airlock with a clatter of magnetic boots and a hiss of pressure equalization. His face, visible through the helmet visor, was flushed with exertion. He cracked the seal and pulled the helmet off, shaking out dark hair matted with sweat.

"Ship Two flange is ready for closure," he said, leaning against the bulkhead to catch his breath. "O-ring seated, guide pins engaged. When Jonah tightens the bolts on the far side, this tunnel becomes real."

Gabriel stood, feeling the need to do something with his hands. He picked up his recorder and aimed it at Arun, not because he needed to, but because the gesture felt like part of what he was here to do. "How close does it need to be? The alignment, I mean."

"Good question," Arun said, wiping his forehead with the back of his glove. He pulled himself onto the cargo crate beside Gabriel, still breathing hard. "The primary seal—the O-ring—can tolerate maybe six millimeters of offset before it starts to twist. A twisted O-ring is a leak, and a leak is the fastest way to turn this whole operation into a very expensive failure. The tunnel itself is flexible. Those corrugations can stretch and compress, which is why we're using them instead of a rigid tube. But flex has limits. Push too hard and you deform the metal permanently, and then you've got a tunnel that never seals properly, no matter how many bolts you tighten."

"So you're telling me it's a goldilocks problem," Gabriel said. "Too tight, too loose."

Arun smiled faintly. "Exactly that. And we have to do it by hand."

Outside, through the viewport, Gabriel could see Jonah's suit working at the coupling. The movements were slow and deliberate. Every quarter-turn of the bolt required a pause to check the pressure reading, then another turn, another pause. It was the opposite of fast. It was the speed of something that could not afford to be wrong.

"Tell me something," Gabriel said. He kept the recorder running not because he'd play it back later—he would, but that wasn't the point. The point was that by asking the question and recording the answer, he was making the moment part of the record. He was making it real in the way that history is real: spoken, heard, preserved. "When we're done here, when we've got all three ships connected and people walking between them in their socks... what makes it different? I mean, really different. We've got the habitat. We've got the life support. What does the tunnel change?"

Arun considered the question with the seriousness it deserved. He looked out the viewport at the tunnel, at the two ships it connected, at the thin pink sky beyond.

"Pressure," he said simply. "That's what it changes. Pressure."

Gabriel waited.

"Outside," Arun continued, tapping the glass with his knuckle, "the atmospheric pressure on Mars is about six to ten millibars. On Earth, at sea level, it's a thousand and thirteen. So the air out there—" he gestured at the landscape beyond the hull "—is less than one percent as thick as what we're breathing right now. That difference sounds like a number until you understand what it means for physics."

He paused, organizing his thoughts. Gabriel waited. This was the part of being a historian that he loved: watching smart people translate expertise into plain language, watching knowledge become shared knowledge.

"At six millibars," Arun said, "liquid water cannot exist in the open. It's too thin. If you poured a cup of water onto the Martian surface, it would boil and freeze at the same time. The pressure is so low that the water molecules can't hold each other together long enough to stay liquid. They either turn to vapor or turn to ice, depending on the temperature. So everything that depends on liquid water—every biological process, every chemical reaction we rely on, every seed in Mei's greenhouse—only exists inside these ships. Not because the water can't handle the cold. It could, if it were frozen. But liquid water needs pressure. And we are the ones providing it."

He turned to Gabriel, and his expression was intense.

"This whole base is a bubble, Gabriel. A bubble of borrowed Earth. We're pressing against the outside world with every square centimeter of hull. One hundred kilopascals pushing out against less than one kilopascal pushing in. That's the difference between life and nothing. And the tunnel we're building right now extends that bubble. It makes the space between ships part of the same pressurized volume. So when it holds, we're not just connecting two buildings. We're making more room for the bubble to expand."

Gabriel lowered the recorder. He felt the weight of what Arun had just said—not the technical details, which he understood intellectually, but the emotional truth beneath them. A bubble of borrowed Earth. He thought about his daughter, back home, about the last time he'd held her hand. He thought about how the sky outside was the wrong color and the gravity was wrong and the air was wrong, and everything about Mars insisted that humans did not belong here.

And yet, they were pressing their bubble against the surface, millibars of pressure and inches of aluminum, and saying they did.

Outside, Jonah drove the final bolt home. The coupling ring tightened with a metallic groan that vibrated through Ship Two's floor plates. Arun stood up, his eyes going to the pressure display on the wall.

"Moment of truth," he said quietly.

---

The first thing Gabriel noticed was the light.

It was red. Not the warm red of a sunset, not the red of warning indicators or emergency lighting, but the cold, thin red of a single LED on Arun's diagnostic panel, blinking with a frequency that seemed almost alive. It was the kind of light that, in a dark room, draws your eye and holds it, demanding your attention, refusing to be ignored.

The pressure transducer had gone red.

"Misalignment," Arun said, his voice flat. "The bolt sequence pulled the ring unevenly. We've got a gap on the lower quadrant."

Jonah's voice came over the comms, sharp with alarm. "I feel it. There's a hiss. Arun, I feel air."

*Mission AI: "Pressure decline detected in tunnel volume. Rate: point zero three bar per second. At current leak rate, full hull equalization with external environment will occur in approximately four minutes. Recommend immediate abort and reseal."*

The word *abort* landed in Ship Two's cabin like a stone in still water. Its ripples reached every person who heard it.

Gabriel felt his chest tighten. He was not an engineer. He could not fix a coupling. But he understood what the red light meant: everything they had spent the last three hours building was coming apart. The tunnel was leaking. If they lost the seal, they lost the connection, and the connection wasn't just convenience. It was the proof that the colony could build something larger than a single ship. It was the first act of construction, not just survival.

Arun was already moving. He grabbed the diagnostic tablet from its mount and ran to the viewport, his eyes scanning the coupling ring. Through the glass, he could see the forward flange at a slightly wrong angle—a fraction of a degree of tilt that meant the O-ring wasn't compressing evenly. The lower section was pinched too tight while the upper section gaped open by a millimeter. It was barely visible. But it was enough.

"Jonah," Arun said, his voice rapid but controlled. "Back off bolts seven through ten. Two turns each, counterclockwise. We need to release the lower tension before the upper can seat properly."

Outside, Jonah rotated the bolts with a torque wrench, his movements urgent but not panicked. One turn. Two turns. Seven. Eight. Nine. The tension eased.

*Mission AI: "Leak rate decreasing. Point zero two bar per second. Point zero one five. The abort sequence may no longer be necessary if reseating is successful. I recommend continuing manual correction. Commander, you have approximately one hundred and eighty seconds before tunnel pressure drops below minimum operational threshold."*

"Arun!" Elena's voice, sharp as wire. "Status."

"We're reseating," Arun said. "Jonah released lower tension. Now I need to take up on the upper bolts to pull the ring down into even contact. But if I over-torque, I'll crush the upper O-ring and make it worse."

Gabriel watched Arun's hands on the tablet. They were steady, but the data stream they were reading was not. The pressure curve flickered between red and amber, a heartbeat in trouble.

One hundred and fifty seconds.

Arun moved to the upper coupling controls. He turned the first bolt a quarter turn. The pressure stabilizer held. Second bolt, quarter turn. Holding. Third bolt. The light flickered green for half a second, then back to amber.

"Come on," Arun whispered.

Outside, the dust was picking up. The storm, still many hours away, was already announcing itself with a thin veil of particles that turned the sky a deeper, more hostile red. Gabriel could feel the fine vibration through the floor plates—the wind was moving the dust, the dust was moving against the hull, and the hull was moving against the tunnel. Everything was connected now, even the problems.

One hundred seconds.

Jonah's voice: "I'm at the midpoint of my bolt cycle. How's pressure looking?"

"Still leaking," Arun said. "But slower. Keep going."

He turned another bolt. The amber light held. Another bolt. Amber. Another. The light flickered, went red, went amber again.

*Mission AI: "At this rate, reseal must be achieved within approximately forty-five seconds. Commander, I recommend preparing emergency sealant injection as a backup measure."*

"Ready the sealant," Elena said. Inside Ship One, she had her hand on the emergency valve for the quick-setting polymer that could flood the coupling and create a temporary bond. It was messy and would complicate later maintenance, but it would stop the leak.

Arun turned the final upper bolt.

The pressure transducer held steady on amber for a long moment. Gabriel watched it the way a patient watches a heart monitor, unable to look away, unable to interpret the numbers but desperate to read the color.

Amber.

Then green.

The red light went out.

Gabriel didn't realize he'd been holding his breath until his lungs demanded it back. He let it out in a rush.

*Mission AI: "Tunnel pressure stabilizing. Leak rate at zero point zero zero two bar per second, consistent with normal permeation through the O-ring material. Not a structural leak. Recommend monitoring for the next thirty minutes, but coupling integrity is restored."*

"Seal holds," Arun said, and the relief in his voice was so plain that Gabriel wanted to smile. Instead, he raised the recorder to his mouth and said nothing. He just let it run. Some moments didn't need commentary. They needed witnesses.

---

The cheer started in Ship Two.

It began with Arun—a short, sharp burst of laughter that erupted before he could stop it. Then Gabriel joined in, not because the moment demanded celebration but because his body needed to release the tension that had been building for three hours. The cheer moved through Ship Two's cabin, bouncing off the bulkheads, and over the comms it reached Ship One, where it found Jonah, who added his own voice—a rough, gravelly sound that spoke of someone more accustomed to the grating of tools than the release of joy.

Elena let herself smile. It was a small thing, a crack in the discipline she wore like armor, but it was real. She unstrapped from her station and pressed her hand against the airlock glass again, looking through at the tunnel—a corrugated silver spine connecting Ship One to Ship Two, holding its pressure, holding the colony together.

*Mission AI: "All systems nominal. Tunnel coupling integrity confirmed. Internal pressure between ships is equalized at one hundred point one kilopascals. The connection is stable."*

"It's stable," Elena repeated to the crew. "We have a tunnel. People can walk between Ship One and Ship Two without suits. Supplies can move on carts. Mei's greenhouse supplies can reach the lab without three airlock cycles."

The cheer grew. It was not the triumphant roar of a sports crowd. It was something smaller and more honest—the sound of people who had been working under the weight of possibility, who had felt the red light and the seconds ticking down and the knowledge that Mars does not forgive mistakes, and who had survived it. The cheer was a release valve, and they opened it together.

Jonah came through the inner airlock of Ship One, his suit still dusty from the exterior work, his helmet under his arm. He crossed into the main cabin and the first thing he did was remove his gloves and touch the bulkhead with bare hands.

"Feels different," he said quietly.

Arun came from Ship Two, also helmetless, his hair a wreck, his face marked with the red imprint of his helmet seal. He stood beside Jonah, and the two men looked at each other across the deck plates.

"You pulled a good bolt sequence," Arun said.

"You read a good diagnostic," Jonah replied. They nodded at each other, the engineer's equivalent of an embrace, and sat down on the cargo crate Gabriel had been occupying an hour ago.

Gabriel recorded it all. The cheer fading into exhaustion. The dust on Jonah's boots. The way Arun's hands trembled, just slightly, from adrenaline. The way the tunnel, visible through each ship's viewport, looked ordinary now. Already ordinary. That was the miracle: the miraculous becoming mundane, the achievement becoming infrastructure.

Imani Sato floated into the cabin from the forward corridor, her boots clicking rhythmically against the deck. She was the pilot and field operations lead, the one who had flown all three ships through their descent, and she carried herself with the easy confidence of someone who trusted her own hands. She took one look at the tunnel through the viewport and raised a hand.

"Nice work," she said. "When do we get the third one?"

The room's temperature dropped by several degrees. Not literally. But Gabriel felt it. The cheer that had filled the cabin a minute ago lost its breath.

*Ship Three.* The third ship, the one that had landed tilted on its side, its landing strut driven deep into sediment, its hull at an angle that made tunnel connections nearly impossible without first jacking the entire structure level. They had been working on that problem for two sols, and the solution—hydraulic jacks, regolith redistribution, a carefully planned lift sequence—was still days away.

"Soon," Elena said, and her voice carried the careful tone of a commander who was honest but protective. "Tomas has the modeling done. We start the lift sequence once we've verified the tunnel connection holds through the next dust event. I won't connect Ship Three until I know Ship One and Ship Two are stable."

"Understood," Imani said. But Gabriel heard the frustration beneath her words, quiet but real.

He saw it too—already forming. The crew that lived in Ship One and Ship Two was about to become a connected community. They could share meals in one mess hall, pool their supplies without crossing the regolith, sit and talk in the same pressurized space. Ship Three's crew—Imani, two engineers, and the medical officer, Laila Okonkwo—would remain isolated. Not abandoned. Never that. But separated by something that wasn't just distance.

The social geometry of the colony was about to change, and the tilt of one ship's hull would determine who was inside the bubble and who was, at least for now, outside it.

Gabriel made a note in his archive. *Sol 9. First tunnel connected. Second tunnel pending. Third ship remains isolated. The colony has its first fault line.*

---

Laila Okonkwo was already awake when the cheer reached Ship Three. The ship's interior was tilted at fifteen degrees, which meant everything rested at an angle that the human body could tolerate but never forget. Water poured from bottles in an oval stream. People slept at a slant, propped against pillows that had been arranged to create the illusion of flatness. The dining alcove had to be secured with magnetic straps so that plates didn't slide into the adjacent bulkhead during meal service.

Laila sat on her bunk, listening to the cheer through the comms, and smiled. She was a physician and ethicist, a woman who had spent her career considering what owed was owed between people and what people owed to each other. She had signed up for this mission because she believed that the medical practice of the future had to be practiced in the future—that treating humans on another world would require a different kind of medicine, one that understood the psychological weight of distance and the physical strain of alien gravity.

The cheer made her happy because it meant the tunnel had held. Her patients—or future patients, since no one had needed serious medical attention yet—could now move between ships without the stress of suit-up procedures. The tunnel meant faster response times, simpler evacuations, reduced exposure to environmental hazards. From a medical standpoint, it was everything she could have asked for.

But then she heard the silence that followed.

The silence told her about Ship Three. It was the silence of inclusion, of hearing a celebration that wasn't quite yours. It was the subtle pain of proximity without participation, of seeing something being built and knowing you weren't inside it yet.

Laila made her way down the tilted corridor to the medical bay, her body compensating automatically for the angle. In the med bay, she checked the supply inventory—bandages, antibiotics, trauma kits, diagnostic equipment. All present. All accounted for. Her job, for now, was to wait.

She sat at her workstation and opened a personal log. Not the official mission log that would be transmitted to Earth, but the private notes she kept as an ethicist on a mission whose ethical boundaries had not yet been drawn.

*Sol 9,* she wrote. *The tunnel between Ship One and Two is connected. Congratulations are in order, and the crew deserves them. But I am already thinking about Ship Three. Isolation is not just physical. It is social, emotional, and political. The crew here is functioning well, but I can feel the distance growing—not across the regolith, which is only fifty meters, but in the shared experience of the colony. When Ship One and Two can share a meal without EVA suits, and we cannot, we become the outside crew. And being the outside crew, even for a few days, will shape how this colony understands itself.*

She paused, her stylus hovering above the screen.

*A colony that forms with an internal border is already forming with an internal hierarchy. I don't believe Commander Varga intends this. I don't believe anyone intends it. But intentions are not architecture, and the architecture of this base—who lives where, who is connected to whom, who walks freely and who walks in suits—will define the colony's social structure long before any charter or compact is written.*

She saved the note and closed the log. Through Ship Three's primary viewport, she could see the tunnel stretching between the other two ships—a silver thread in the red landscape, small and fragile and already part of the base's anatomy. It was beautiful. And it made her uneasy.

Outside, the wind was picking up. The dust storm was still hours away, but its advance was visible as an ochre haze that thickened the horizon. Laila watched the tunnel through the haze and wondered whether it would hold.

In Ship One's comms station, Gabriel Winter was watching the same haze through a different viewport, and thinking the same thought.

Earth was twenty minutes away by radio signal. A photon traveling at the speed of light, carrying a voice, a message, a command from Mission Control in Houston. Twenty minutes each way. Forty minutes for an exchange. In the time it took Earth to hear from them and respond, Gabriel had time to walk the length of Ship One twice, check his archive system, and read three pages of a novel he'd downloaded before launch.

Twenty minutes should have made Earth feel close.

But it didn't.

Instead, the radio silence had started to feel like a wall. The messages coming through were routine—status requests, health queries, agency pleasantries—but the gaps between them were growing. The dust storm on Earth's end, or something else, was disrupting the signal array. Gabriel could see the gaps in his comms log: where there should have been three transmissions per sol, there were now two. Then one today.

Earth was still there, technically. The signal delay hadn't changed. The light-speed limit hadn't shifted. But the connection was thinning, and as it thinned, Gabriel felt something stranger than distance.

He felt the colony beginning to think of itself as separate.

Not separate from Earth, not yet. That would come later, in chapters he could already see approaching. But separate in a new way. The tunnel made Ship One and Ship Two a single place. A place that wasn't Earth and wasn't quite Mars, either. A bubble of borrowed Earth, as Arun had called it, but a bubble that was beginning to feel less like a borrowed thing and more like something being built in earnest.

With the habitat linked, Earth should feel closer.

Instead it starts to feel strange.

*End of Chapter 3 — Bridge: With the habitat linked, Earth should feel closer. Instead it starts to feel strange.*
